explanations.explanation: Kill. That's the word the text uses: Ishbi-benob resolved to kill David. No negotiating and no warm-up chat. I think a worn-out king is the last person who should be on that man's list.

Capturing would mean David stays alive, and the text doesn't say that. It says Ishbi-benob resolved to kill him. He's bearing a bronze spear and a new sword, and I think that's not the gear of a man planning a polite pickup. The word you want is kill.

A challenge is a lot of talking, and the text gives Ishbi-benob no speech here. It says he resolved to kill David. Taunting does show up later in this passage, with a different man at Gath, but not with this one. So the word is kill.

Abishai it is. He comes to David's aid, strikes the Philistine and kills him. He's the son of Zeruiah, and the text gives us no more about him here. I think David was mighty glad to see him show up, because a tired man can only duck so fast.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada is one of David's mighty men, a valiant man from Kabzeel (2 Samuel 23:20). He's a real fighter, so it's a fair guess. But in this scene the text names Abishai son of Zeruiah as the one who comes to David's aid. Benaiah doesn't get a mention here.

Ittai the Gittite is a man from Gath who told David he'd stay with him, whether for death or for life (2 Samuel 15:21). That's a loyal man, so I see why he came to mind. In this moment, though, the text says Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid. Ittai isn't named in this scene.

explanations.answer: He must never go to battle with them again
explanations.explanation: That's the oath. David's men swear, "You must never again go out with us to battle…" It's a firm line, and I bet it came out of a very tense moment. They don't ask nicely, either. They swear it.

explanations.answer: They will always fight right beside him
explanations.explanation: It sounds loyal, and these men are loyal, but it's not what they swear. The text has them tell David, "You must never again go out with us to battle…" So the oath is about David staying out of the fight. Standing beside him isn't in it.

explanations.answer: He must lead them from the very front
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what they say. David just ended up exhausted with a spear-carrying man coming for him. So they swear, "You must never again go out with us to battle…" The men want him away from the front line, not at it.
True. The text says Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. That's the same family line as Ishbi-benob. Rapha's descendants keep turning up in these battles.

It's actually True. The text says Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. Ishbi-benob is also called a descendant of Rapha, so they share that family line. The name Rapha keeps coming back as the battles go on.

Yes, Goliath the Gittite. Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite kills his brother at Gob. Goliath is the famous Philistine champion from Gath whom David struck down (1 Samuel 17:4, 50). So this brother has a very big name hanging over him.

Achish was the king of Gath, the place David once went to when he was on the run (1 Samuel 21:10). So it's a name that fits the neighborhood. But the text says Elhanan killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite. Achish isn't mentioned here.

Abimelech king of Gerar shows up way back with Abraham's household (Genesis 20:2). He's a king in a Philistine-area story, so I get the mix-up. In this passage, though, Elhanan son of Jair kills the brother of Goliath the Gittite. Abimelech isn't in it.

It's actually False. The text says this man of great stature at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. Armor isn't mentioned at all. Armor you can take off, and this man couldn't.

False, and good catch. The text never mentions bronze armor on this man. It says he had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. Count that out slowly and you'll see why they remembered him.

explanations.answer: Jonathan son of David's brother Shimei
explanations.explanation: That's him. When the man at Gath taunts Israel, Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei kills him. So this Jonathan is David's nephew. A taunt is a risky thing to say when family like that is standing nearby.

explanations.answer: Amasa son of David's sister Abigail
explanations.explanation: Amasa is a relative of David, and 1 Chronicles 2:16-17 names Abigail as David's sister and Amasa's mother. So the family tie is real. But in this scene the text says Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei kills the man. Amasa isn't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: Absalom son of David's wife Maacah
explanations.explanation: Absalom was David's son by Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3). He's famous, so his name comes to mind fast. But here the text gives the credit to Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei. Absalom has no part in this battle.

Four. The text sums it up: "So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants." Count them with me: Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath's brother and the man with twenty-four fingers and toes. It all adds up.

Three is one short. Ishbi-benob, Saph and the man with the extra fingers and toes make three, but Goliath's brother is also in the list. That makes four, and the text says it too: "these four descendants of Rapha." So the list is a little longer than it feels.

Five is one too many. The text counts them up as "these four descendants of Rapha in Gath." That's Ishbi-benob, Saph, the brother of Goliath the Gittite and the man with six fingers on each hand. Four names and then the tally, no extra.
